code.title: HashMap get(key): spread the hash, pick the bucket, walk the chain
code.python:
CAP = 16                                   # capacity is a power of two
table = [[] for _ in range(CAP)]           # each bucket: list of (hash, key, value)


def spread(h):
    return h ^ (h >> 16)                   # mix the high bits into the low bits


def put(key, value):
    h = spread(key)
    table[h & (CAP - 1)].append((h, key, value))   # index = hash AND (capacity - 1)


def get(key):
    h = spread(key)
    i = h & (CAP - 1)
    checked = 0
    for eh, ek, ev in table[i]:            # walk the chain in that one bucket
        checked += 1
        if eh == h and ek == key:          # compare stored hash first, then the key
            print(f"get({key}): bucket {i}, checked {checked} entries, value {ev}")
            return
    print(f"get({key}): bucket {i}, checked {checked} entries, not found")


# Time: O(1) average per get/put, O(chain length) in one bucket. Space: O(N).
keys = [17, 33, 1, 65552]
print(f"keys = {keys}, capacity = {CAP}")
for k in keys:
    put(k, k * 10)
get(33)
get(65552)
get(49)
get(5)

followUps:
Because comparing two int values is one cheap machine instruction, while equals() can be slow, so the map uses the hash as a quick filter.

Each node keeps the hash it was inserted with. If the stored hash differs from the hash of the key you are looking for, the two keys cannot be equal, so equals() is skipped. Only when the hashes match does the map pay for the real comparison.

Example: a bucket holds three 1,000-character strings. Without the filter a lookup may compare thousands of characters three times. With it, the two wrong entries are rejected by one integer comparison each, and equals() runs once, on the real match. The cost is 4 extra bytes per node. It also means a resize never has to call hashCode() again.

A HashMap accepts one null key and always stores it in bucket 0.

The internal helper is (key == null) ? 0 : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16), so hashCode() is never called on null and nothing throws. The comparison in the chain is k == key || (key != null && key.equals(k)), so null matches by reference.

Example: map.put(null, 1); map.put(null, 2); leaves one entry with value 2, and map.get(null) returns 2.

Other maps differ: Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap throw NullPointerException for a null key, and a TreeMap with natural ordering does too, because it must call compareTo. Also remember that get returning null can mean "no such key" or "key mapped to null"; use containsKey to tell them apart.

Because with a power-of-two capacity the bucket index can be found with one fast AND instead of a slow division, and a resize becomes very simple.

  • Speed: hash & (capacity - 1) gives the same result as hash % capacity for non-negative values. With capacity 16 the mask is 1111 in binary, so hash 37 (100101) lands in bucket 5. The AND also never gives a negative index, which % does for negative hashes in Java.
  • Resize: doubling adds exactly one bit to the mask, so every key either stays at index i or moves to i + oldCapacity. No full recomputation is needed.

The price: only the low bits pick the bucket, so hashes that differ only in high bits would collide. That is why Java first mixes the bits with h ^ (h >>> 16). If you ask for capacity 100, Java rounds it up to 128.

code.title: Equal objects with different hashes: the set cannot find its own element
code.python:
next_id = 0


def point(x, y):
    # A point is [x, y, id]. The id is different for every object, like a memory address.
    global next_id
    next_id += 1
    return [x, y, next_id]


def same(p, q):
    return p[0] == q[0] and p[1] == q[1]            # plays equals()


def hash_of(p, use_fields):
    return 31 * p[0] + p[1] if use_fields else p[2] * 7   # good hash uses x and y; bad one uses the id


def demo(label, use_fields):
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(8)]
    a, b = point(1, 2), point(1, 2)
    buckets[hash_of(a, use_fields) % 8].append(a)   # add(a)
    chain = buckets[hash_of(b, use_fields) % 8]
    found = any(same(p, b) for p in chain)          # contains(b) searches b's bucket only
    if not found:
        chain.append(b)                             # add(b) stores a "duplicate"
    size = sum(len(c) for c in buckets)
    print(f"{label}: contains(b) = {'yes' if found else 'no'}, size after add(b) = {size}")


# Time: O(1) average per add/contains. Space: O(N).
print("a = (1, 2), b = (1, 2), a equals b: yes")
demo("hash ignores the fields", False)
demo("hash uses the fields", True)

followUps:
Because the map files an entry under the hash the key had when it was inserted; if you change the key afterwards, its hash changes and the map looks in the wrong bucket.

Example: a List<Integer> key [1, 2] has hash 994, so with 16 buckets it sits in bucket 2. Now call key.add(3): the hash becomes 30,817, which points to bucket 1. map.get(key) searches bucket 1, finds nothing and returns null, although the entry is still inside the map. containsKey and remove fail the same way, so the entry can never be removed by key (a memory leak), yet it still shows up when you iterate.

The hashCode is perfectly correct here; the bug is the mutation. Use immutable keys: String, Integer, records, List.copyOf(...), tuples in Python. If a key must change, remove it, change it, then put it back.

Yes, it is legal, because equal objects still get equal hash codes (everything gets 42); it is just extremely slow.

The contract only demands "equal objects, equal hashes". It does not demand that different objects get different hashes. But with a constant hash every key lands in the same bucket, so the map turns into one long chain:

  • each get, put or remove walks the chain: O(N) instead of O(1);
  • inserting N keys costs 1 + 2 + … + N comparisons, which is O(N2). For 100,000 keys that is about 5 billion comparisons instead of 100,000;
  • Java 8 turns a long chain into a red-black tree, which improves this to O(log N) per operation, but only works well if the keys are Comparable.

So the result stays correct and the performance is lost. A constant hash is sometimes used on purpose in tests to force collisions.

code.title: Good hash vs all keys colliding: count the comparisons
code.python:
N, CAP = 1000, 1024


def comparisons(all_collide):
    # Insert keys 0..N-1, then look every key up and count key comparisons.
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(CAP)]
    for key in range(N):
        index = 0 if all_collide else key & (CAP - 1)   # a bad hash sends everything to bucket 0
        buckets[index].append(key)
    count = 0
    for key in range(N):
        index = 0 if all_collide else key & (CAP - 1)
        for stored in buckets[index]:                   # walk the chain until the key is found
            count += 1
            if stored == key:
                break
    return count


# Good hash: O(1) per lookup, O(N) in total. All colliding: O(N) per lookup, O(N^2) in total.
# Space: O(N + capacity).
print(f"N = {N} keys, {CAP} buckets")
print(f"good hash: {comparisons(False)} comparisons for {N} lookups")
print(f"all keys collide: {comparisons(True)} comparisons for {N} lookups")

followUps:
The attacker sends one request that contains thousands of keys chosen in advance to have the same hash, so the server's map degrades into one long chain while parsing it. This is called a hash-flooding or HashDoS attack.

Web frameworks put form fields, query parameters, headers and JSON keys into a hash map. If the hash function is public and fixed, collisions are easy to build. In Java, "Aa" and "BB" both hash to 2112, so "AaAa", "AaBB", "BBAa", "BBBB" all collide, and 16 such pairs glued together give 216 = 65,536 colliding keys. Inserting N colliding keys costs O(N2): one small POST can burn minutes of CPU.

Defences: a hash seeded with a random secret per process (SipHash in Python, Rust, Ruby), Java 8 turning long chains into trees (O(log N) worst case), and limits on the number of parameters and on body size.

Because iteration has to look at every bucket, empty or not, so its cost depends on the capacity of the table and not only on how many entries are in it.

The cost is O(capacity + size). A Java HashMap never shrinks: if it once held 1,000,000 entries its table has 2,097,152 buckets (the next power of two above 1,000,000 / 0.75). Remove all but 10 entries and a for loop over it still scans about 2 million slots to find those 10. clear() keeps the big table too.

Fixes:

  • copy the survivors into a fresh map, new HashMap<>(old), which is sized for the current number of entries;
  • use LinkedHashMap, which links the entries together and iterates in O(size) whatever the capacity.

Lookups are not affected: get still goes straight to one bucket in O(1).

code.title: Resize from 8 to 16 buckets: every key stays at i or moves to i + 8
code.python:
# Time: O(N) to move N keys during one resize. Space: O(new capacity).
old_cap, new_cap = 8, 16
keys = [3, 11, 19, 27, 5, 13]
threshold = old_cap * 3 // 4                  # load factor 0.75: grow when size > 6
print(f"keys = {keys}")
print(f"capacity {old_cap}, grows when size > {threshold}")

stayed = moved = 0
for key in keys:
    old_index = key & (old_cap - 1)           # uses the low 3 bits of the hash
    new_index = key & (new_cap - 1)           # uses the low 4 bits: one extra bit
    moves = (key & old_cap) != 0              # that extra bit decides: stay or move
    if moves:
        moved += 1
    else:
        stayed += 1
    note = f"(moves by {old_cap})" if moves else "(stays)"
    print(f"key {key}: index {old_index} -> {new_index} {note}")

print(f"stayed: {stayed}, moved: {moved}")

followUps:
It sets the starting number of buckets, not the number of entries the map can hold; Java rounds 100 up to the next power of two, 128, and the map still resizes once it holds more than 128 × 0.75 = 96 entries.

So new HashMap<>(100) followed by 100 puts triggers one resize (to 256 buckets) at the 97th entry, which is the very thing you wanted to avoid.

To hold N entries with no resize, ask for N / 0.75 + 1:

Map<String, Integer> m = new HashMap<>(134);   // 100 / 0.75 + 1, rounded up to 256 buckets

Java 19 added HashMap.newHashMap(100), which does this calculation for you. Also note that the bucket array is created lazily, on the first put, so an empty pre-sized map costs almost nothing.

No. A Java HashMap only ever grows; removing entries, even all of them with clear(), keeps the bucket array at its largest size.

Example: put 1,000,000 entries and the table grows to 2,097,152 buckets, about 8 MB of references with compressed pointers. Remove 999,990 of them and the table is still 2,097,152 buckets. Two things suffer: the memory stays allocated, and iteration still scans every bucket, O(capacity).

The designers chose this because shrinking would cost an O(N) rehash and a map that was big once often becomes big again. To get the memory back, build a new map from the old one: map = new HashMap<>(map);.

One thing does shrink: a bucket that had been turned into a tree goes back to a linked list when it drops to 6 entries or fewer. C++ unordered_map also keeps its buckets on erase; Python dicts shrink only when a later insert triggers a resize.

code.title: Open addressing with linear probing, and why deletes need a tombstone
code.python:
EMPTY, TOMB, SIZE = -1, -2, 8
table = [EMPTY] * SIZE


def insert(key):
    i = key % SIZE
    while table[i] != EMPTY and table[i] != TOMB:   # slot taken: try the next one
        i = (i + 1) % SIZE
    table[i] = key


def find(key):
    i = key % SIZE
    for _ in range(SIZE):
        if table[i] == EMPTY:                       # a truly empty slot ends the search
            return -1
        if table[i] == key:
            return i
        i = (i + 1) % SIZE                          # tombstones are skipped, not stopped at
    return -1


# Time: O(1) average per operation at low load, O(N) worst case. Space: O(capacity), no nodes.
for k in (1, 9, 17):                                # all three want slot 1
    insert(k)
print(f"after insert 1, 9, 17: {table}")
slot = find(9)
table[slot] = TOMB                                  # correct delete: leave a marker
print(f"delete 9 with a tombstone: find(17) = {find(17)}")
table[slot] = EMPTY                                 # wrong delete: breaks the probe chain
print(f"delete 9 by emptying the slot: find(17) = {find(17)}")

followUps:
You cannot simply empty the slot; you either leave a "deleted" marker called a tombstone, or you shift the following entries back to close the gap.

The reason: a search stops at the first empty slot. Suppose keys 1, 9 and 17 all hash to slot 1 in a table of 8, so they sit in slots 1, 2 and 3. If deleting 9 just empties slot 2, a search for 17 starts at slot 1, reaches the empty slot 2 and wrongly reports "not found".

  • Tombstone: mark slot 2 as deleted. Searches skip over it; inserts may reuse it. Too many tombstones slow every search, so the table is rebuilt from time to time.
  • Backward shift: after removing, move each later entry of the same run one slot back if that keeps it reachable from its home slot. No markers, but the delete does more work.

Both are O(1) on average at a moderate load.

Because in open addressing every collision is resolved by probing other slots of the same array, and the number of probes rises very steeply as the array fills up.

For a search that misses, the expected number of probes is about 1 / (1 − α), where α is the fraction of slots in use:

Load αExpected probes
0.502
0.663
0.9010
0.99100

A chained table degrades gently (a chain of 2 instead of 1), but an open-addressed table has no chains to absorb the overflow, and a completely full one cannot insert at all. So CPython grows a dict once it is two-thirds full. The empty third costs little, because Python's compact dict keeps the entries in a separate dense array and the sparse table holds only small indices.

code.title: Count subarrays with sum K using prefix sums and a hash map
code.python:
def count_subarrays(arr, k):
    # Time: O(N), one pass. Space: O(N) for the map of prefix sums.
    seen = {0: 1}                         # the empty prefix has sum 0 and occurred once
    prefix = 0
    answer = 0
    for x in arr:
        prefix += x
        answer += seen.get(prefix - k, 0)   # earlier prefixes that leave exactly k
        seen[prefix] = seen.get(prefix, 0) + 1   # insert after the query, never before
    return answer


arr = [3, 4, -7, 1, 3, 3, 1, -4]
k = 7
print(f"arr = {arr}, K = {k}")
print(f"subarrays with sum {k}: {count_subarrays(arr, k)}")
print(f"with K = 0: {count_subarrays(arr, 0)}")

followUps:
Store the remainder of each prefix sum instead of the prefix sum itself: a subarray's sum is divisible by K exactly when the prefix before it and the prefix at its end leave the same remainder.

  1. Keep a map (or an array of size K) remainder → how many prefixes had it, seeded with remainder 0 seen once.
  2. For each element, update the prefix, take its remainder, add the current count of that remainder to the answer, then increase the count.
  3. Make the remainder non-negative, because % can return a negative value in Java, C++ and JavaScript.
cnt[0] = 1;
for (int x : arr) {
  prefix += x;
  int r = ((prefix % k) + k) % k;
  answer += cnt[r]++;
}

Example: [4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1], K = 5 gives remainders 4, 4, 4, 2, 4, 0 and the answer 7. Time O(N), space O(K).

Fix a pair of rows (top and bottom), squash the rows between them into one array of column sums, and run the 1D "subarrays with sum K" method on that array.

  1. For each top row, start a column-sum array of zeros.
  2. For each bottom row from top downwards, add that row into the column sums.
  3. Count the subarrays with sum K in the column sums using the prefix map seeded with {0: 1}. Each one is a rectangle between top and bottom.
for (int top = 0; top < R; top++) {
  int[] col = new int[C];
  for (int bot = top; bot < R; bot++) {
    for (int c = 0; c < C; c++) col[c] += m[bot][c];
    total += countSubarrays(col, k);
  }
}

Example: [[1, 1], [1, 1]] with K = 2 gives 4 (two rows of width 2, two columns of height 2). Time O(R2 · C), space O(C); loop over the smaller dimension in the outer pair.

The map stores the first index where each prefix sum appeared instead of how many times it appeared, and the seed becomes {0: −1}.

For each end index i, a start is valid if an earlier prefix equals prefix − K. To make the subarray as long as possible you want the earliest such prefix, so you record an index only the first time a prefix sum is seen and never overwrite it.

first.put(0, -1);
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  prefix += arr[i];
  if (first.containsKey(prefix - k)) best = Math.max(best, i - first.get(prefix - k));
  first.putIfAbsent(prefix, i);
}

Example: [1, -1, 5, -2, 3], K = 3. Prefixes are 1, 0, 5, 3, 6. At index 3 the prefix is 3, and 3 − 3 = 0 was first seen at −1, so the length is 3 − (−1) = 4. Time O(N), space O(N).

code.title: Longest subarray with sum K, with and without the {0: -1} seed
code.python:
def longest(arr, k, seed):
    # Time: O(N). Space: O(N) for the map prefix sum -> first index.
    first = {0: -1} if seed else {}       # the empty prefix sits just before index 0
    prefix = 0
    best = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(arr):
        prefix += x
        if prefix - k in first:           # earliest place where the rest sums to k
            best = max(best, i - first[prefix - k])
        first.setdefault(prefix, i)       # keep the earliest index only
    return best


arr = [1, 2, 3, 7]
k = 6
print(f"arr = {arr}, K = {k}")
print(f"with seed {{0: -1}}: longest = {longest(arr, k, True)}")
print(f"without the seed:  longest = {longest(arr, k, False)}")

followUps:
Any input whose answer starts at index 0 fails; the smallest example is [3, 4] with K = 7.

Trace it without the seed. After 3 the prefix is 3; we look for 3 − 7 = −4 in the map: absent. After 4 the prefix is 7; we look for 7 − 7 = 0: also absent, because nobody stored the "sum before any element". The code returns 0 subarrays, but [3, 4] itself sums to 7, so the right answer is 1.

With the seed {0: 1} the second lookup finds 0 once and the answer is 1.

Two more quick failures:

  • zero-sum check on [2, -2]: the prefixes are 2 and 0, no prefix repeats, so without 0 in the set the code says "no zero-sum subarray";
  • longest subarray with sum 6 in [1, 2, 3]: without {0: −1} the answer is 0 instead of 3.

The seed is still {0: −1}, the empty prefix just before index 0; what changes is that the map keeps the latest index of each prefix sum instead of the first.

For the shortest subarray ending at i you want the start as far right as possible, so you overwrite the stored index every time a prefix sum is seen again:

last.put(0, -1);
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  prefix += arr[i];
  if (last.containsKey(prefix - k)) best = Math.min(best, i - last.get(prefix - k));
  last.put(prefix, i);   // overwrite: keep the newest
}

Example: [1, 2, -2, 2, 1], K = 3. At index 1 the prefix is 3 and matches the seed: length 2. At index 4 the prefix is 4, and prefix 1 was last seen at index 2, so the length is 2 again. Without the seed the first match would be missed. Start best at infinity. Time O(N), space O(N).

code.title: Insert, delete and getRandom in O(1): array plus hash map, swap with the last
code.python:
import random

values = []        # gives O(1) random access
index_of = {}      # value -> its index in the list


def insert(v):
    if v in index_of:
        return False
    index_of[v] = len(values)
    values.append(v)
    return True


def remove(v):
    if v not in index_of:
        return False
    i = index_of[v]
    last = values[-1]
    values[i] = last           # move the last element into the hole
    index_of[last] = i         # and record its new index
    values.pop()               # removing the last item needs no shifting
    del index_of[v]
    return True


def get_random():
    return values[random.randrange(len(values))]


# Time: O(1) average for all three operations. Space: O(N).
for v in (10, 20, 30, 40):
    insert(v)
print(f"after insert 10, 20, 30, 40: {values}")
remove(20)
print(f"after remove 20: {values}")
print(f"index of 40 in the map: {index_of[40]}")
print(f"getRandom returned a current member: {'yes' if get_random() in index_of else 'no'}")

followUps:
Keep the same list of values, but change the map so that each value points to the set of all positions where it sits in the list.

  1. Insert: append the value to the list and add its position to the value's set. Always succeeds.
  2. Remove: take any one position i from the value's set. Move the last list element into position i, and in that element's set replace "last position" with i. Then pop the list, and delete the value's map entry if its set is now empty.
  3. getRandom: pick a random list position, as before.
int i = idx.get(val).iterator().next();
idx.get(val).remove(i);
int last = list.get(list.size() - 1);
list.set(i, last);
idx.get(last).add(i);
idx.get(last).remove(list.size() - 1);

Then remove the last list slot. The order of the add and remove on last's set matters when i is the last position. All operations stay O(1) on average; a value stored 3 times is returned 3 times as often.

If every copy of a value occupies its own slot in the list, getRandom is already weighted by frequency: a value stored 3 times out of 10 slots is picked with probability 3/10, and nothing needs to change.

If you store each value once with a weight (a count), you need a different pick:

  • Prefix sums + binary search: for weights 5, 1, 4 the prefix sums are 5, 6, 10. Draw a random number from 1 to 10 and find the first prefix that is ≥ it: 1–5 gives the first value, 6 the second, 7–10 the third. A pick is O(log N), but changing one weight costs O(N) to rebuild.
  • Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) over the weights: both a weight update and a pick are O(log N). This is the usual answer when inserts and deletes keep happening.
  • Alias method: O(1) picks after O(N) setup, for weights that never change.

code.title: Lost updates: check-then-act interleaving vs one atomic step (simulated)
code.python:
# Two workers each add 1 three times. We replay, on one thread, the order of steps
# that two real threads can produce, so the result is the same on every run.


def unsafe_count():
    hits = {"home": 0}
    for _ in range(3):
        a = hits["home"]          # worker A reads the count
        b = hits["home"]          # worker B reads the same old count
        hits["home"] = a + 1      # A writes
        hits["home"] = b + 1      # B overwrites A's update: one increment is lost
    return hits["home"]


def atomic_count():
    hits = {}

    def add_one(key):             # read + add + write as one step
        hits[key] = hits.get(key, 0) + 1

    for _ in range(3):
        add_one("home")           # worker A
        add_one("home")           # worker B sees A's result
    return hits["home"]


# Time: O(1) per update. Space: O(number of keys).
unsafe = unsafe_count()
print(f"6 increments, read and write interleaved: count = {unsafe} ({6 - unsafe} lost)")
print(f"6 increments, each one atomic: count = {atomic_count()}")

followUps:
Because in a map shared by threads a null result would be ambiguous: you could not tell "this key is absent" from "this key is present and its value is null".

In a single-threaded HashMap you can settle it with a second call: if (map.containsKey(k)) v = map.get(k);. In a concurrent map another thread can remove or insert the key between those two calls, so the pair is not reliable and there is no way to ask both questions at once.

By banning nulls, one call gives a clear answer: get(k) == null always means "no mapping right now". The atomic methods rely on this too: putIfAbsent returns null to say "I inserted it", and computeIfAbsent treats a null result as "store nothing". Null keys are banned for the same reason. If you need "no value", store an explicit marker such as Optional.empty().

Use a ConcurrentHashMap and make each increment one atomic step: either merge, or a LongAdder per key when many threads hit the same keys.

// simple and correct
counts.merge(key, 1L, Long::sum);

// faster under heavy contention
ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> hits = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
hits.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new LongAdder()).increment();
long total = hits.get(key).sum();

What does not work is counts.put(key, counts.get(key) + 1): two threads can both read 5 and both write 6, losing one event, even though each single call is thread-safe.

merge locks one bin for the update, so threads counting the same hot key queue up. LongAdder spreads the count over several internal cells, so writers rarely collide, and adds the cells up when you call sum(). The sum is not an exact snapshot while writes continue, which is normally fine for metrics.

code.title: Longest consecutive sequence: count how often the inner loop really runs
code.python:
# Time: O(N) average. Space: O(N) for the set.
nums = [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2, 2]
values = set(nums)
best = 0
inner_steps = 0

for x in values:                      # loop over the set, so duplicates are visited once
    if x - 1 in values:               # x is not the front of a run: skip it
        continue
    length = 1
    while x + length in values:       # walk the run starting at its front
        length += 1
        inner_steps += 1
    best = max(best, length)

print(f"nums = {nums}")
print(f"longest run of consecutive values: {best}")
print(f"inner loop steps in total: {inner_steps} (N = {len(nums)})")

followUps:
Keep a map that stores, for the two end points of every run seen so far, the length of that run; each new number then joins its left and right neighbours in O(1).

  1. If the number x was already seen, ignore it.
  2. Read left = length of the run ending at x − 1 and right = length of the run starting at x + 1 (0 if absent).
  3. The merged run has length left + right + 1. Write that length at its two ends, x − left and x + right, and update the best.
if (len.containsKey(x)) return best;
int l = len.getOrDefault(x - 1, 0), r = len.getOrDefault(x + 1, 0);
int total = l + r + 1;
len.put(x, total);
len.put(x - l, total);
len.put(x + r, total);
best = Math.max(best, total);

Example: stream 1, 3, 2. After 1 and 3 there are two runs of length 1. Adding 2 gives l = 1, r = 1, total 3, stored at 1 and 3. Time O(1) average per number, space O(N). Union-Find also works.

Sorting is the better choice when the input is small or medium, when memory matters, or when you need the sorted data afterwards anyway.

  • Speed in practice: sorting an int[] runs over memory in order and is very cache-friendly. A HashSet<Integer> allocates an object per element and jumps around the heap. For up to a few million numbers the O(N log N) sort often finishes sooner than the O(N) hash version.
  • Memory: an in-place sort needs O(1) or O(log N) extra space. A Java hash set needs roughly 40 to 50 bytes per number, against 4 bytes in the array.
  • Predictability: the sort has a guaranteed O(N log N) worst case; the hash set can degrade with bad or hostile keys.
  • Simplicity: sort, then one pass: extend the run if a[i] == a[i-1] + 1, skip if equal, otherwise restart at 1.

Say this trade-off out loud, and use the hash set when the interviewer requires O(N) or the array must not be changed.

code.title: Small fixed alphabet: a 26-slot array instead of a hash map
code.python:
# Time: O(N) for a word of N letters. Space: O(1), always 26 counters.
word = "swiss"
count = [0] * 26                        # one slot per letter: no hashing needed
for c in word:
    count[ord(c) - ord("a")] += 1

parts = []
for i in range(26):                     # the array is already in alphabetical order
    if count[i] > 0:
        parts.append(f"{chr(ord('a') + i)}={count[i]}")

first_unique = "none"
for c in word:                          # second pass in the word's own order
    if count[ord(c) - ord("a")] == 1:
        first_unique = c
        break

print(f"word = {word}")
print(f"letter counts: {' '.join(parts)}")
print(f"first letter that appears once: {first_unique}")

followUps:
Roughly 48 to 70 bytes per entry on a 64-bit JVM with compressed pointers, to store just 8 bytes of real data (two ints).

PartBytes
Node object (header 12, hash 4, key, value and next references 4 each, padding)32
Integer key object (header 12 + int 4)16
Integer value object16
Slot in the bucket array (4 bytes ÷ load of 0.375 to 0.75)5 to 11

That is about 70 bytes, or about 8 times the raw data. Values from −128 to 127 come from a shared Integer cache, which lowers the figure for small numbers. One million entries therefore need about 70 MB, where two int[] arrays need 8 MB. Each lookup also follows three pointers, which is slow on the CPU cache. This is why an int[] or a primitive map library is preferred for large numeric data.

A Bloom filter saves a lot of memory by giving up certainty: it may say "probably present" for an item that was never added, but it never says "absent" for an item that was added.

It is a bit array with k hash functions. Adding an item sets k bits; a lookup checks those k bits. If any is 0 the item is definitely absent. If all are 1 the item is probably present, because other items may have set those bits.

The trade-off is memory against the false-positive rate, which is about (1 − e−kn/m)k for n items in m bits:

  • about 10 bits per item with 7 hashes gives roughly 1% false positives;
  • each extra 4.8 bits per item cuts the rate by a factor of 10.

So 100 million keys fit in about 120 MB instead of several GB for a hash set. Costs: you cannot list or delete items (deleting needs a counting Bloom filter), and the rate grows if you add more items than planned. Typical use: skip a disk or network lookup when the filter says "absent".

code.title: Minimum window substring with a need[] tally and a missing counter
code.python:
def min_window(s, t):
    # Time: O(|s| + |t|), each pointer only moves forward. Space: O(1), a 128-slot table.
    need = [0] * 128
    for c in t:
        need[ord(c)] += 1
    missing = len(t)
    left = best_start = 0
    best_len = float("inf")
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        c = ord(ch)
        if need[c] > 0:
            missing -= 1                 # this character was still required
        need[c] -= 1                     # extra copies go negative
        while missing == 0:              # window covers t: record it, then shrink
            if right - left + 1 < best_len:
                best_len = right - left + 1
                best_start = left
            d = ord(s[left])
            left += 1
            need[d] += 1
            if need[d] > 0:
                missing += 1             # we just dropped a required character
    return "" if best_len == float("inf") else s[best_start:best_start + best_len]


s, t = "ADOBECODEBANC", "ABC"
w = min_window(s, t)
print(f"s = {s}, t = {t}")
print(f"smallest window: {w} (length {len(w)})")
print(f"t = AABC: {min_window(s, 'AABC')}")

followUps:
Nothing special is needed: need holds a count per character, not a yes/no flag, so if t contains a character twice the window must contain it twice.

For t = "AABC": need[A] = 2, need[B] = 1, need[C] = 1, and missing = 4 (the length of t, duplicates included). Reading the window:

  • first A: need[A] is 2 > 0, so missing becomes 3 and need[A] becomes 1;
  • second A: 1 > 0, missing becomes 2, need[A] becomes 0;
  • third A: 0 is not > 0, so missing is unchanged and need[A] becomes −1, meaning one spare A.

When shrinking, removing an A raises need[A] from −1 to 0, still not positive, so the window stays valid; only removing a needed copy makes it positive and increases missing. The common bug is to set missing to the number of distinct characters while still decrementing per character.

Treat each word as one "character": count the words you need in a map, and slide a window that moves one whole word at a time. This works when all words have the same length L (the usual version of the problem).

  1. Build need: word → count.
  2. A word can start at any position, so run the scan L times, once for each start offset 0, 1, …, L − 1.
  3. In one scan, read the next L characters as a word and add it to a have map. While that word's count exceeds what is needed, remove words from the left. A word that is not in need resets the window.
  4. When the window holds exactly the required number of words, record its start.

Example: s = "barfoothefoobarman", words ["foo", "bar"], L = 3: offset 0 reads bar, foo, the, foo, bar, man and finds matches at indices 0 and 9. Each scan touches every word once, so the total is O(|s|) word reads, each costing O(L) to cut and hash. Space O(number of words).

code.title: Group anagrams with a 26-count key (separators included)
code.python:
def key_of(word):
    # Key = the 26 letter counts joined with '#', for example "1#0#0#0#1#...".
    count = [0] * 26
    for c in word:
        count[ord(c) - ord("a")] += 1
    return "".join(f"{n}#" for n in count)   # the separator keeps 1,11 apart from 11,1


# Time: O(N * K) for N words of length K. Space: O(N * K).
words = ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat", ""]
groups = {}                                  # a dict keeps first-seen order
for w in words:
    groups.setdefault(key_of(w), []).append(w)   # anagrams share a key

print("words: " + " ".join(words) + "(last one is the empty string)")
number = 1
for g in groups.values():
    print(f"group {number} ({len(g)}): [{', '.join(g)}]")
    number += 1

followUps:
Use as the key the list of gaps between neighbouring letters, taken modulo 26; two strings are shifts of each other exactly when all their gaps match.

Shifting every letter by the same amount does not change the difference between consecutive letters. So:

  • "abc" has gaps 1, 1 and "xyz" has gaps 1, 1: same group;
  • "az" has gap 25; "ba" has gap −1, and (−1 + 26) % 26 = 25: same group, because the alphabet wraps around;
  • "acef" has gaps 2, 2, 1 and belongs to another group.
StringBuilder key = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 1; i < s.length(); i++) {
  int gap = (s.charAt(i) - s.charAt(i - 1) + 26) % 26;
  key.append(gap).append('#');
}
groups.computeIfAbsent(key.toString(), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(s);

Keep the separator, otherwise gaps 1, 12 and 11, 2 give the same text. All single-letter strings get the empty key and form one group. Time O(total characters), space the same.

Then the cost is dominated by building the key for each long word, so use the counting key, which is linear in the word length, instead of the sorted key.

With K = 100,000 letters and N = 10 words:

  • sorting key: K log K is about 100,000 × 17 = 1.7 million steps per word, 17 million in total, and each key is a 100,000-character string that the map must also hash and compare;
  • counting key: one pass of 100,000 steps per word, 1 million in total, and the key is only 26 numbers.

With only 10 words you do not even need a hash map: compute the 26 counts for every word (O(N · K)) and compare the count arrays pairwise, 45 pairs × 26 comparisons. Memory matters too: avoid keeping sorted copies of the words, which would double the 1 MB of input. A quick first filter is the word length, since anagrams must have equal length.

code.title: Hashing Point(x, y): x + y collides, 31 * x + y does not

followUps:
Because 31 is an odd prime that is cheap to multiply by and spreads typical keys well enough; there is nothing magic about it beyond that.

  • Odd: multiplying by an even number shifts bits out on overflow and loses information. Multiplying by 2 throws away the top bit every time. An odd multiplier is reversible modulo 232, so no information is lost.
  • Cheap: 31 * h equals (h << 5) - h, a shift and a subtraction, which mattered on old CPUs and which compilers still use.
  • Position matters: each field is multiplied a different number of times, so order counts. With 31 * x + y, (1, 2) gives 33 and (2, 1) gives 63, while x + y gives 3 for both.

It is not collision-free: "Aa" is 65 × 31 + 97 = 2112 and "BB" is 66 × 31 + 66 = 2112. Other odd multipliers such as 17, 37 or 1,000,003 (used by Python tuples in older versions) work equally well.

Put x in the upper 32 bits and y in the lower 32 bits of one long; every pair of ints then gets its own unique number, so there are no collisions between different points.

long key = ((long) x << 32) | (y & 0xFFFFFFFFL);
int x2 = (int) (key >> 32);   // unpack
int y2 = (int) key;

Two details matter. Cast x to long before shifting, otherwise the shift happens in 32 bits and x is lost. Mask y with 0xFFFFFFFFL, otherwise a negative y is sign-extended and its 1-bits overwrite x. Example: x = 1, y = −1 gives 0x00000001FFFFFFFF with the mask, but −1 without it.

This avoids a small object per key and suits primitive long maps; in a HashMap<Long, V> the key is still boxed. For a small grid, x * width + y is simpler. In JavaScript, numbers are only exact up to 253, so use x * 100003 + y for small ranges, a string key, or BigInt.

code.title: Unique visitors in a sliding window: map of user -> count in the window
code.python:
def unique_per_window(visits, window):
    # Time: O(N), each visit is added once and removed once. Space: O(window).
    in_window = {}                       # user id -> visits inside the window
    result = []
    for i, user in enumerate(visits):
        in_window[user] = in_window.get(user, 0) + 1    # the new visit enters
        if i >= window:
            old = visits[i - window]                    # the oldest visit leaves
            in_window[old] -= 1
            if in_window[old] == 0:
                del in_window[old]                      # drop keys at 0
        if i >= window - 1:
            result.append(len(in_window))               # map size = unique users
    return result


visits = [7, 7, 8, 7, 9, 9, 9, 9]
window = 4
print(f"visits (user ids) = {visits}, window = {window}")
print(f"unique visitors per window: {unique_per_window(visits, window)}")

followUps:
Because a HyperLogLog sketch recognises a user it has already seen, while a plain number does not remember who was counted, so adding numbers counts returning users twice.

Example: minute 1 has visitors {a, b, c}, so its exact count is 3. Minute 2 has {b, c, d}, also 3. Adding gives 6, but the real number of different visitors is 4, because b and c came back. To get 4 exactly you need the two sets themselves, which is the expensive part.

A HyperLogLog sketch keeps a few thousand small registers. Each user is hashed; the hash picks one register and that register stores the largest "number of leading zeros" seen so far. The same user always hashes to the same register and the same value, so seeing them again changes nothing. Merging two sketches is taking the larger value in each register, which gives exactly the sketch you would get from the combined stream. A merge costs O(number of registers), about 12 KB of work, whatever the traffic.

Do not use the sketches for billing; write every raw event to durable storage during the day and run an exact "count distinct" batch job over it at the end of the day.

  1. Log: append each visit (user id, timestamp) to a durable log such as Kafka, then to files in object storage. The real-time HyperLogLog path stays as it is for dashboards.
  2. Split: the nightly job sends each event to a partition chosen by hash(userId) % P. The same user always lands in the same partition.
  3. Deduplicate: each partition is small enough to fit in memory, so it puts its user ids in a hash set (or sorts them) and counts the distinct ones.
  4. Add: sum the partition counts. This is valid here because no user appears in two partitions.

Example: 50 million users in 64 partitions is under 1 million ids per partition, a few tens of MB each. The job is O(events) time, runs in minutes, and can be re-run from the log if someone disputes a bill.
